paragraphs: I've worked in Moraga long enough to know that a well-positioned home on a quiet cul-de-sac with mature fruit trees and a finished two-car garage doesn't come along every season, and 206 Sheila Ct caught my attention the moment it hit the market. The combination of a thoughtfully updated interior, a generous 10,450-square-foot lot, and that proximity to the trail network is exactly what a certain kind of Lamorinda buyer has been waiting for. When the listing came off the market after 21 days without a sale, I wanted to reach out, because I don't think the home is the issue.

Twenty-one days is short enough that it might feel like bad luck, but in my experience it usually points to something more specific. At $885 per square foot, this home is priced at the upper end of the Moraga range, and that number is supportable given the condition and the lot. The problem is that supporting a number like that requires marketing that builds the case for it, visually and narratively, before a buyer ever schedules a showing. A description that reads as a competent list of features is not the same thing as a story that makes a qualified buyer feel certain they're looking at the right home. I think the listing had the first, but not the second.

I've put together a short packet that walks through three specific areas where the strategy fell short and what a relaunch would look like if we addressed each of them directly. It's not a pitch to re-list at a lower number. It's an honest look at the gap between what this home is worth and how it was positioned.
If you're already working with an agent toward a new listing, please feel free to disregard this entirely. If you're not, I'd welcome a brief call to walk through what I've found.

exec_summary.headline: A Refined Cul-de-Sac Home with Genuine Premium Assets  -  and a Listing That Left the Case Unmade
exec_summary.p1: 206 Sheila Ct has the fundamentals that Lamorinda buyers at this price point are actively looking for: a flexible four-bedroom floor plan with a main-level guest suite, an updated kitchen with double ovens and stone counters, a finished two-car garage with sealed flooring and built-in storage, and a 10,450-square-foot lot with a private backyard framed by mature fruit trees. The home sits near top-rated schools and direct trail access, which are two of the most consistent buyer motivators in the Moraga market. These are real, defensible assets.
exec_summary.p2: The listing history doesn't reflect those assets. At $885 per square foot, this home is priced at the upper tier of the Moraga market, which is justified by its condition and lot size, but that justification has to be built explicitly in the marketing. The listing spent 21 days active without converting, which suggests the strategy reached buyers but didn't persuade them. The description catalogued the home's features without giving buyers the visual depth or narrative confidence to act at that price. A standard MLS approach doesn't close that gap.
exec_summary.p3: A relaunch needs to do one specific thing: give qualified buyers at the $1.69M level the visual evidence and the narrative to justify the premium before they arrive at the front door. The home earns the number. The strategy has to prove it.

forensics.title: Friction #1: Premium Priced at $885/sqft, but the Marketing Never Justified the Number
forensics.body: At $885 per square foot, 206 Sheila Ct sits above the top of the standard updated Moraga range, which runs to roughly $820 per square foot. That's not a flaw  -  the finished garage, updated kitchen, double ovens, stone counters, and 10,450-square-foot lot are all real differentiators that support a premium. But buyers comparing this home against others in the $1.6M to $1.7M range need to understand specifically what they're getting at that number that they can't find down the street. The listing described the features. It never built the argument. When buyers can't answer their own 'why is this worth more' question, they don't make offers  -  they keep looking.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork uses Zillow Showcase placement to tell a structured premium story directly on the portal page where buyers are already comparing  -  not buried in remarks, but in the framing buyers see first.

forensics.title: Friction #2: The Visual Story of This Lot Was Never Told
forensics.body: A 10,450-square-foot cul-de-sac lot with a private backyard, brick patio, separate side yard, and mature fruit trees is not a standard Moraga offering. It's a specific kind of space that photographs poorly with ground-level MLS angles and satellite thumbnails. Buyers scrolling listings at this price range don't register 'grassy lawn and fruit trees' from a flat wide-angle  -  they need to see the lot in context: the setting, the privacy, the scale, the street position. Without that, the outdoor space reads as a line item rather than the premium it actually represents. A buyer who might have stretched to $1.69M for a yard like this probably kept scrolling.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's Sky Tour captures the lot position, street setting, and private backyard in a way ground photography simply cannot  -  giving buyers the spatial context to understand what they're actually getting before they ever schedule a showing.

forensics.title: Friction #3: The Right Buyers Were Never Actively Found
forensics.body: At $1,690,000, the buyer pool is real but narrow. These are typically move-up buyers from Oakland or San Francisco, or Lamorinda families relocating within the market, who are doing serious online research before they commit to a showing. In that environment, passive MLS distribution is not enough. The buyers who remain active at this price point are selective and well-informed, and they need to encounter this home in the right context  -  not just on a standard listing feed, but in targeted placements that reach them while they're actively thinking about Moraga. This listing was available to those buyers, but it wasn't built to find them.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork runs geo-targeted digital campaigns that put this home directly in front of SF and East Bay buyers who are already researching Lamorinda  -  reaching the decision-maker before they've settled on another property.

positioning_table.verdict: At $885/sqft versus a benchmark range of $750-$820/sqft, this home sits near the upper end of that range. At $885 per square foot, this home is priced above the top of the Moraga premium tier, which tops out near $820 per square foot for well-updated homes. The lot size, finished garage, updated kitchen, and no-HOA status are all legitimate supports for a premium, but the gap between the asking price and the top of the market benchmark means the marketing had to work harder than a standard listing to close the distance. That case was never fully made, and that's the gap a relaunch needs to close.

pillars.title: Pillar I  -  Build the Visual Case for the Lot Before Buyers Arrive
pillars.body: The backyard, the fruit trees, the brick patio, and the cul-de-sac position are the kind of assets that move buyers at this price point  -  but only if they can see them clearly before they schedule a showing. Standard ground photography doesn't capture a 10,450-square-foot lot in context. A Sky Tour shows buyers exactly what they're getting: the setting, the privacy, and the scale that separates this home from comparable inventory. Buyers who understand the outdoor space before they visit are more motivated and more prepared to make a confident offer.

pillars.title: Pillar II  -  Tell a Premium Story That Justifies $885 per Square Foot
pillars.body: Every detail in this home  -  the double ovens, the stone counters, the finished garage, the main-level guest suite, the built-in storage  -  adds up to a premium that is real and defensible. The marketing needs to present those details as a coherent argument, not a checklist. BrightWork writes listing remarks and structures portal placement the way a great buyer's agent explains a home: with logic and specificity, so the buyer can answer their own 'why this one' question before they ever talk to their agent. That's what turns a showing into an offer at the right number.

pillars.title: Pillar III  -  Find the Right Buyer Actively, Not Passively
pillars.body: The buyer for 206 Sheila Ct is likely a Bay Area family who has been researching Lamorinda schools and trail access for months and is ready to move when they find the right home. That buyer isn't waiting for a listing alert  -  they're being researched on Google and Instagram right now. BrightWork's geo-targeted campaigns are built to reach that buyer where they already are, in Moraga-specific context, before they've committed to another property. The goal isn't more clicks. It's the right buyer, found early, arriving at the door already sold on the neighborhood.
